28_interl8: concerning the knowledge of divine things
28_marg9: The parables bring this profit: that through them it may be known what is to be believed, and whither the intent of the heart is to be directed, and what is to be done while men live on earth, so that in thought and in deed man may return to heaven.
28_interl9: So that it is not enough for those who have been taught that they once received knowledge and learned to serve the discipline of the virtues; but let them listen to the words of the prudent, by which they may become more perfect
28_interl11: concerning the ordering of temporal things
28_marg10: What profit they have is shown in the title, when it says: to know wisdom and instruction; that is, how each ought to believe and live rightly, and whither to direct the intent of the heart.
28_interl13: Objection: a mover is not moved, therefore knowledge is not known. Reply: the things that belong to wisdom are known, that is, by faith, namely the articles; so too the gloss resolved it of the ordering of temporal things
28_interl14: by which they may make progress
28_interl15: of the prudent in divine things
28_marg11: To understand the words of prudence: that is, let them not only embrace the wisdom they have received and serve the discipline of the virtues, but also listen to the words of prudence, by which they may make progress, and understand them skilfully.
28_interl16: let them understand with the heart what is said, and take up the manner of life of the teachers shown beforehand in deed
28_interl17: of the teachers in worldly things
28_marg12: by which we work well according to the rule of truth
28_interl18: that we may deal with our neighbours with right discernment
28_interl19: that with a sincere intention, in the things we rightly do or judge, we may strive to please God alone
28_interl20: who have lately lent their ear to wisdom
28_marg13: Subtilty, which is needful to beginners, so that they may be able to beware the craftiness of sophistries, lest they be drawn away from the simplicity of wisdom, which leads to life.
28_marg14: To the young man, in the singular, because wisdom, though it receives men of different kinds, leads them on by its teaching into one perfection of virtue. Whence in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul.”
28_marg15: To the young man, namely, because he who wisely turns aside from what is false will fittingly receive the knowledge of the truth.
28_interl24: even from those lesser than he, while he lays up in his heart whatever of profit he hears
28_marg16: A wise man shall hear. He fitly begins with wisdom, because, when the choice was given him, he asked for wisdom and received it.
28_marg17: A wise man shall hear. He shows that no one in this life is so wise that he cannot become wiser even by the sayings of lesser men. The queen of Saba heard Solomon, the lesser hearing the greater, and went home wiser. Moses heard his father-in-law, a man far beneath him, and was made wiser.
28_interl26: of his own life and another’s
28_marg18: And he that understandeth. Let no one boast of his own knowledge; for he who neglects to hear the words of the wise does not know how to govern his own life, much less another’s. So when he says “A wise man shall hear and shall be wiser”, it looks to the knowledge of the things that are known through wisdom; but “he that understandeth shall possess governments” looks to the rightness of life; and it agrees with the title, where it is said: “To know wisdom and instruction”, etc.
28_interl28: this Christ gave to his disciples, that they might understand his parables and the riddles of the law
28_interl29: which says one thing and means another
28_marg19: The fear of the Lord, etc. Bede. There are two fears of the Lord: the servile, which is the beginning of wisdom or knowledge; and the friendly, which goes with the perfection of wisdom. The servile is the beginning of wisdom, because he who begins to be wise after his errors is first checked by the fear of the Lord, lest he be punished. But this “perfect charity casteth out”. After it comes the holy fear of the Lord, “enduring for ever and ever”, which charity does not shut out but increases: by which a son fears to offend the eyes of a most loving Father even in the least thing. This indeed will cease in the world to come, but “charity never falleth away”.
28_marg20: Wisdom and instruction. He said: “A wise man shall hear”, etc. He says the contrary of fools: that the wisdom of right teaching and the instruction, that is, the discipline, of pure living, they not only do not attain but even scorn to know.
28_interl35: as the Pharisees despised the sayings and deeds of Christ
28_marg21: Despise. In the plural, because fools are more than the wise; and the company of all the wise is of one mind, while the life and teaching of those who err are unlike. Whence in the singular: “A wise man shall hear”, etc.
28_interl37: for so we ought to love God and obey him, and serve the unity of the Church with brotherly charity
28_marg22: Thus far he has spoken in proverbs of both sides; from here he earnestly warns each of the faithful to put the discipline of the divine law before the coaxing of the reprobate, because on one side is the crown, on the other eternal death. And so he calls him son, whom he is careful to instruct as a father.
28_marg23: Since it is said in the person of God the Father, the mother is the Church, which was then called the Synagogue; or the grace of God itself, for among the Hebrews the Spirit, who gives grace, is called by the feminine word ruha.
28_interl39: charity of mind, that it may be more ardently kindled
28_marg24: To those who kept the law of the Lord, at the coming of Christ, was added the grace of the New Testament with the hope of the heavenly kingdom, whose surpassing splendour is like a crown, or like a chain of gold, closed by no end. To us also, when for the good things which divine grace bestowed beforehand, eternal light is given, grace is, as it were, added to the head and a chain to the neck. Whence: “We have received grace for grace”, namely the grace of blessed reward for the grace of right working.
28_interl40: as is the custom for him who strives lawfully, so for us also
28_marg25: The brightness of perfect working, for the preaching which goes forth through the neck, which it strengthens with an unfailing bond of virtues.
28_marg26: He speaks to his son with a father’s affection, coaxing him not to consent to sinners.
28_interl44: either urging to do evil, or praising what is done with applause; wisdom keeps us from both
28_marg27: Either in general of robbers, who lay snares for the innocent; or, spiritually, of those who gave over the author of life to death.
28_marg28: Though in general this belongs to all who lie in wait for blood, yet in particular it belongs to the Jews, who hid snares for the guiltless Lord, and with guile encompassed his apostles, winged with virtues. They acted against their own blood and souls: fearing to lose an earthly kingdom, they killed the King of heaven and persecuted the citizens of heaven on earth. And so they lost both what they had on earth and the kingdom they could have gained in heaven. But in general it must be said that whoever has the eyes of faith open will receive wings from the Lord like a dove, with which to fly to eternal rest; in vain do the wicked weave snares for such, and rather destroy themselves by their presumption.
28_interl49: “Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?”, and the like
28_interl51: for they were harmed by him in nothing; nay, they had known many benefits from him
28_marg29: Innocent. “Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.”
28_interl53: that he may not seem to have lived
28_interl55: “They have laid me in the lower pit”
28_marg30: Let us swallow, etc. Let us blot out the memory of his virtues and teaching, so that it may not be remembered that he even lived among us.
28_interl57: “This is the heir: come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance.”
28_marg31: All precious substance. That is, the men whom they saw cleaving to Christ, whom they thought to part from his love and company if they killed him, and to fill their houses with the spoils of such, that is, their gatherings with their souls.
28_marg32: Cast in thy lot, etc. Of robbers in general it is plain, for they promise a share of the plunder to the fellows they gather. But the persecutors of Christ also joined to themselves whomever they could; those whom they saw following him they put out of the synagogue, that is, deprived of their communion.
28_interl64: one must not walk with the ungodly
28_interl65: believing Christ to be God, do not hold communion with the Jews who persecute him. Whence Peter: “Save yourselves from this perverse generation.”
28_marg33: Run to evil. Not only to what they will do, but to what they will suffer for what they have done. For the more they hasten to accomplish the crime, the nearer they draw to bearing the penalty for the crime.
28_interl66: he easily escapes the snare on the earth who has his eyes in heaven
28_interl67: the snare of persecution, or wrong teaching
28_marg34: In vain, etc. The rest was of the plotters against Christ in particular; this is of the faithful in general. In vain is the snare of persecution or of death spread for the elect, who have the wings of hope and charity and the other virtues, with which they desire heavenly things while they live and reach them after death. They have also the eyes of the mind, with which they foresee that the evils they suffer will pass, the good things they merit will last for ever, the pride of the reprobate will end, and their torments will last for ever.
28_marg35: Or by the net is meant the wrong teaching which he spoke of from the place where he says: “If sinners shall entice thee”. This is spread in vain before those who look upon things above with the eyes of the heart, who say with the prophet: “Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers.”
28_interl69: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
28_interl70: that they may be punished with temporal death
28_interl71: that their souls may be punished with eternal damnation
28_interl72: the subtle thoughts by which he takes care to increase his money
28_marg36: So the ways. Not only do those who watch for plunder and the slaughter of the innocent destroy themselves; but likewise the thoughts of every covetous man, which put gold before God, drag him to destruction.
28_marg37: Otherwise: So the ways of every covetous man, etc. As I said before, every covetous man destroys or strips those who abound in possessions, so that he himself rather perishes. For in the poor he has nothing to go after.
28_marg38: Wisdom. Thus far, the persecutions which the Jews brought upon Christ; from here, what he speaks of his passion, through the apostles, to the same persecutors.
28_marg39: Wisdom, that is, Christ, speaks abroad, that is, openly, in the light, so that, leaving childhood behind, they may be “children in malice”.
28_interl75: they lie in wait for their own blood, but wisdom preacheth abroad
28_marg40: Abroad. Openly after the resurrection, because, when the Spirit was sent, she declared herself through the apostles. For before, she opened the mysteries of the Godhead to few. Whence: “Tell the vision to no man, till the Son of man be risen from the dead.” And she showed her power rather by works, the prophecy being fulfilled: “Neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets.”
28_interl76: in the breadth of the peoples
28_marg41: She uttereth her voice in the streets. What she had taught before a few, she now repeated openly. Whence: “That which I tell you in the dark, speak ye in the light.”
28_interl77: among the princes, whom she reminded of the death of Christ and called to repentance
28_marg42: In the entrance of the gates of the city. The city of the Lord is the Church, gathered from both peoples. The doors of its gates are the preachers, who lead into it. In these she uttered her words when she spoke in the apostles, one of whom says: “Do you seek a proof of Christ that speaketh in me?” Or the doors of the synagogue are the greater saints, in whom wisdom disputed when, speaking through the apostles, she called back the lawyers, the Pharisees and the priests to her grace; so that, as Luke says, “a great multitude also of the priests obeyed the faith”.
28_marg43: How long. You have now seen Christ in the flesh, seen him working miracles, whom you spurned and killed; now at least love him raised from death, and he will forgive what you have sinned.
28_interl82: Now that the New Testament shines out, how long will you put the Old before it, Moses before Christ, the law before the gospel, the precepts given to the unlearned through a servant before those given to the perfect through the Son?
28_interl86: love not childishness, but turn ye
28_marg44: Turn ye, etc. “Wisdom exhorts them to turn to God, and utters the Spirit.”
28_interl87: through the apostles, because they would not believe
28_marg45: At my reproof, etc. Through the apostles she reproves the Jews, and, at least after the ascension and resurrection, warns them to turn.
28_interl88: and if you still neglect it
28_marg46: My spirit, that is, vengeance. Whence: “Thou sentest thy spirit, and the sea covered them.” And in Job: “I have seen the wicked perish by the blast of God, and consumed by the spirit of his wrath.”
28_interl91: by which I foretold your ruin
28_interl92: “Come to me, all you that labour”
28_interl93: I not only called, but stretched out
28_interl94: first by doing good, setting free all who were oppressed by the devil; afterwards on the cross
28_marg47: You have despised. “Woe to you scribes and Pharisees”, etc. In general, “he that doth not believe, is already judged”.
28_marg48: “You have confounded the counsel of the poor man: but the Lord is his hope.”
28_interl97: which are wont to strike terror
28_marg49: I also. So in the Psalm: “He that dwelleth in heaven shall laugh at them: and the Lord shall deride them.” Not that he laughs or derides with cheeks or nose; but so is signified the power which he gave the apostles, by which they foresaw that the ungodly would do nothing against him by their plots except what he permitted, that all their undertakings would come to nothing, and that his glory after the passion would be spread through the whole world. And so they scorned their pride as nothing, even when they saw it at its strongest.
28_interl99: wisdom threatens those who despise her
28_marg50: Which you feared, etc. They feared, saying: “If we let him alone so, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come, and take away our place and nation.”
28_marg51: When sudden calamity shall fall on you. He means the sudden siege of Jerusalem and the conquest of the whole province by the Romans. Of which: “Seeing the city, he wept over it.”
28_marg52: When … shall come upon you. This whole rebuke of wisdom can be taken in general of all the reprobate: that in the day of judgement they will cry to the Lord, asking that the door of the kingdom be opened to them, and will not be heard. For what follows, “they shall rise in the morning and shall not find me”, signifies the time of judgement, when some shall rise to life, others to everlasting reproach.
28_marg53: Tribulation and distress. When the saints suffer without, they are enlarged in heart by a sure hope of salvation. Whence the prophet: “When I called upon him, the God of my justice heard me: when I was in distress, thou hast enlarged me.”
28_marg54: Shall they call. We do not read that the Jews called upon the Lord in the siege; and if any called, they were not heard, because they did not truly repent.
28_interl106: they not only did not have it, but persecuted it with hatred
28_interl107: the correction of morals, or of mine
28_interl108: which is the beginning of wisdom
28_marg55: Hated, etc. The just man, on the contrary: “I have hated the unjust,” he says, “and have loved thy law.”
28_interl109: when I counselled them; whence they are without excuse
28_interl112: because they disparaged and did not consent
28_marg56: Therefore they shall eat. Because they would not walk in my ways so as to live, they will receive the wages of their own ways, so as to perish for ever. But on the contrary, of those who fear the Lord: “Blessed are they that walk in his ways. Thou shalt eat the labours of thy fruits: blessed art thou, and it shall be well with thee.”
28_interl113: of which above: “Their feet run to evil”
28_interl114: they would not be filled with mine
28_marg57: With their own devices. By which they said: “Let us hide snares for the innocent”; by which they chose a robber instead of the Saviour, so that they were laid waste by robbers and damned among robbers. This, like the rest, can be taken of all who despise the word of God.
28_marg58: The turning away. Turning away and prosperity destroy when the soul, turned away from the fear of its Maker, seems to suffer nothing adverse from that same Maker’s wrath in the things in which it sins; but, as Job says: “They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell.”
28_marg59: Of little ones in understanding. Whence above: “How long will you love childishness?” They could have been perfect in understanding, if they had not turned their ear away from the counsel of wisdom; but because they turn away, they kill themselves.
28_interl119: freedom to act, while nothing holds them back from what they say in their musings: “We shall find all precious substance”
28_interl120: of good works now, then of joys in the reward, where there is nothing adverse
28_marg60: But he that, etc. It can be understood both in this life and in the life to come. For he who serves God perfectly does not fear; nay, he rejoices both in adversity and in death, so that at his entrance into life he is glad, at rest from idle thoughts and from temptations; and when he has passed from the world, he rests in the joy of the hoped-for resurrection.
28_interl122: that thou mayst rest without terror
28_marg61: My son. He notes two things here: that wisdom is of heavenly things, prudence of worldly ones.
28_interl123: wisdom exhorts him to receive her words, namely wisdom and prudence
28_interl124: lest the birds of the air eat the seed by the wayside
28_interl125: with a careful heart. Whence: “Thy words have I hidden in my heart, that I may not sin against thee.”
28_marg62: That thy ear may hearken to wisdom. He does not hear with the ear who takes it in only with the bodily ear and neglects to keep it in memory and fulfil it in deed. But if thou receive the commandments of God with a steady love of learning and keeping them, first hold to the way of humility; for this is what follows: Incline thy heart, etc.
28_marg63: Incline thy heart. Incline it, humble it, cleanse it, that it may become worthy to receive the mysteries. Whence: “Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones”; that is, thou hast hidden them from the proud and revealed them to the humble.
28_interl127: the knowledge of God, by which man is blessed
28_marg64: For if thou shalt call for wisdom. To call upon, that is, to call into ourselves by praying, we ought to do to nothing but the Lord. So when he teaches that wisdom is to be called upon, he shows that he sets before us not just any wisdom, but the very knowledge of God, in the receiving of which is the highest blessedness; according to this: “Now this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.” Note that he urges both to call upon wisdom and to incline our own hearts to know prudence, because the divine help is necessary, and free will ought not to be absent.
28_interl130: with as much care as the covetous seek money; so that if thou seek as carefully as one who will gain boundless and unspeakable riches by her, thou shalt have the reward that follows
28_marg65: And as for a treasure. He who digs for treasure throws away the earth, makes the pit deep, and keeps at it busily until he finds what he seeks. So let him who desires to find the treasures of wisdom throw away from himself every earthly weight, make in himself the pit of humility, and not rest until he finds.
28_interl131: if thou seek with a careful heart
28_marg66: Then shalt thou understand the fear. The friendly fear, which is not the beginning but the perfection of heavenly wisdom, at least in this life. And so perfect love does not cast it out, but makes it abide for ever and ever; and thou shalt find also the knowledge of the Godhead itself, which makes blessed for ever: because the Lord, etc.
28_interl134: it looks back to what was said above, from “For if thou shalt call for wisdom” to “and shalt find the knowledge of God”
28_marg67: Because the Lord giveth. For this reason wisdom, that is, God, is to be called upon to receive wisdom: because it cannot be had from ourselves, but is given by the Lord.
28_marg68: Out of his mouth. By the eternal birth of the Son, of which it is said elsewhere: “I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures.” Or the mouth of the Lord is in the saints. Whence: “The mouth of the Lord hath spoken it.” And out of his mouth knowledge and prudence are born when the Lord sanctifies a human mouth and makes it his own, so that it speaks with knowledge and prudence.
28_interl135: rightness and simplicity are akin and are not separated; so wisdom does not ask for one of them without the other, but keeps and protects those in whom both meet
28_marg69: He will keep. So that in whatever degree of virtue he may help the upright and the simple.
28_marg70: Job was simple and upright: simple through the innocence of meekness, and upright through the caution of discernment. Simple: hurting no one, nay, profiting all; upright: corrupted by no one.
28_interl138: when thou hast called upon wisdom
28_interl139: that thou mayst deal with thy neighbour with right discernment
28_interl140: what is meant by each; as she enlightens thee, the knowledge of no good thing will escape thee
28_marg71: From the evil way. To which they call who say: “Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood”. He speaketh perverse things who is the author of this persuasion.
28_interl144: which is done in the light
28_marg72: Who leave the way. He fitly sets the dark ways against the right way, because this is done in the light and leads to the light. But “every one that doth evil hateth the light, that his works may not be reproved”, and his end is in the exterior darkness.
28_marg73: Who are glad, etc. Because they walk by dark ways and know not whither they go. For if they looked at the punishments they are heading for, they would hold back their steps and chasten their harmful gladness with wholesome weeping.
28_interl148: prudence shall preserve thee, that thou mayst be delivered
28_interl150: lest thou commit adultery, or join the heretics
28_marg74: That thou mayst be delivered from the women, etc. After warning the hearer whom wisdom teaches not to share with robbers, not to run with a thief if he saw one, but to walk rightly and simply, he now warns him not to put his portion with adulterers; of whom this too can be understood in particular: That thou mayst be delivered from the evil way, from the man that speaketh perverse things. What speech is more perverse than persuading to lewdness? This section begins: My son, if thou wilt receive my words, etc.
28_marg75: By the strange woman can be understood the wickedness of the heretics, a stranger to Christ and the Church, which deceives the hearts of the innocent with smooth eloquence and the coaxing of the tongue. Whence: “His words are smoother than oil, and the same are darts.”
28_interl151: “His words are smoother than oil, and the same are darts”
28_interl152: her first husband, or teacher of the faith
28_marg76: And forsaketh the guide. It is plain of the heretical mind too, for it forsakes the teacher from whom it had learned the faith of the Church, and has forgotten the covenant of its God, that is, the Lord’s faith contained in the creed, which it had promised on the day of baptism to keep.
28_marg77: Her covenant, which she made with her husband at the time of the wedding, the Lord being witness, namely that they would keep the faith of chastity to one another; or in baptism.
28_interl153: “Broad is the way that leadeth to destruction”
28_interl154: her manner of life, or her flesh
28_marg78: For … inclineth. All the dealings of the adulteress lead to destruction; and however coaxing and gentle she seems, she will feel in the end no lesser vengeance than those who serve ungodliness openly by robbery. The adulteress’s house can be taken to be her very flesh, in which she lies down to filthiness and lust, which in the judgement will rise again to everlasting death. But the house of the heretics, because it is built upon the sand, even when it seems to stand, is sinking to its fall, and by its own growth, as by certain paths, tends to the company of the ungodly, that is, to the torments of the evil spirits.
28_interl156: not she alone perishes, but all
28_marg79: That go in unto her shall return again. That is, to death, not to the woman. For he who has lain with an adulteress can, with the Lord’s help, return and merit life by repenting. He who has been defiled by heresy can come back to salvation by returning to his senses. But he who has once been seized by eternal death will never return to life. This is against Origen, who promises forgiveness even to the devil, deceived by Isaias saying: “They shall be shut up there in prison: and after many days they shall be visited.” But Isaias signifies only that those now shut up in torments will be visited for a little while at the time of the resurrection, so that, having received their bodies in the judgement, they may be more heavily damned and after the judgement shut up again in fiercer punishments. Though it can also rightly be taken thus: unto her, that is, unto the harlot. Or: they shall not return to her house, because nature, damned or depraved by its own wicked will, has, so far as it goes, no way back by itself, but only by the grace of God, by which it is helped and restored to take hold of the paths of life. For by this he marks the weight of iniquity, so that when anyone returns he may ascribe it not to himself but to the grace of God.
28_interl160: prudence shall preserve thee, that thou mayst walk
28_interl161: in the unity of the right faith, of which the Lord says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” And elsewhere: “No man cometh to the Father, but by me.”
28_interl163: who are to be kept: For they that
28_marg80: For they that are upright, etc. Here he joins the simple to the upright, as above when he says: He will keep the salvation of the righteous, etc. For surely simplicity without uprightness is slack and foolish, and uprightness without simplicity is harsh and hard; but the two virtues joined make a man perfect. But there is this difference: in the one it is shown that the Lord helps those who strive in the present; in the other, that he crowns the victors in the future. For by the name of the earth is meant the Church, which brings forth spiritual fruit to God; in it dwell and continue those who are not parted from its fellowship even by death, but, this life ended, come to that part of it which reigns with Christ in heaven.
28_interl168: this can be understood of a people thus: while it lived rightly, it would remain happily in its own land; but when it sinned, it would be driven out by its enemies
28_marg81: The wicked. It is said spiritually of those who seemed to belong to the land of the Lord, that is, the Church, but are taken away from it: some by open judgement, as the ungodly enemies of the Church, Simon, Arius and Porphyry; others by the secret judgement of God, like many who seem to be good men. By the wicked he means open apostates; by those that do unjustly, all who, having received the sacraments of the faith, fall away from its chastity. But both will be destroyed in the future from the land of the living, because “neither shall the wicked dwell near thee: nor shall the unjust abide before thy eyes”. And rightly, having foretold much of the ways of the good and the wicked, he adds at the close of the end of each, as he did in the foregoing parable, in which he forbade the company of robbers, saying of the end of the wicked: “The prosperity of fools shall destroy them”; of the end of the good: “But he that shall hear me, shall rest without terror.”
28_interl170: wisdom exhorts him not to forget the law and the precepts
28_marg82: From here he teaches that we must persevere in works of mercy, and not trust in our own strength but implore or beg help from God; and in fitting order, after restraining him from credulity and chastening him from lust, he adorns with good deeds the one he instructs.
28_interl171: lest the keeping of the precepts laid upon him should trouble the hearer, he first set out the sure rewards, and so, that is, afterwards, he listed the precepts
28_marg83: Peace, that is, the state of blessedness, of which Isaias says: “His empire shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace.” But to the former people of God also it was given that, when it obeyed the law of God, it lived a long time in the quiet of peace.
28_marg84: Mercy and truth. Let truth, which is to be spoken, never be absent from thy mouth; never mercy, which is to be shown to thy neighbour, from thy deeds. For so it comes about that the mercy and truth of God always follow thee too: mercy to blot out sins, truth to fulfil promises.
28_interl177: let thy voice help thy neighbour
28_marg85: Put them about thy neck. In the throat he suggests the instrument of the voice; in the tables of the heart, the breadth of thought. So let the virtue of mercy and truth, fixed in the root of the mind, be uttered by the voice of the speaker, so that the secrets of the intention may please him who sees in secret, and the service of speech may help our neighbours. And he rightly teaches that the virtues are put about the neck, since the speaker’s voice is commonly formed in the throat: for the voice of preaching flows from within but encircles from without. For the more a man stirs others to work and live well, the more he binds himself by the work of preaching to act well, lest his action pass outside his words, or his life contradict his voice.
28_interl178: let the Lord’s intention delight thee
28_marg86: And thou shalt find grace. He finds grace and good understanding before the Lord who by the constant practice of the virtues merits from the Lord to be found more perfect and better than himself day by day. But he also finds grace and good understanding before men by whose works the Father is rightly praised, and who gives his neighbours an example of living.
28_interl179: but fear not that thou canst not keep them
28_interl180: we must have confidence in God, not hesitate in prayer, not trust in our own prudence
28_interl181: not in thyself, not in thy own strength, not in natural knowledge
28_marg87: Have confidence in the Lord. Fear not that, because of thy weakness, thou canst not keep the divine commandments. Nor again think that thou canst fulfil them by thy own strength, or know them by thy natural knowledge, if thou art not instructed by his law; but rather seek his help both in speaking and in acting, and he will grant thee to be able to fulfil what he has commanded.
28_interl182: by setting thyself before the fathers
28_interl183: in the things thou hast received from the fathers, as though more learned than the rest
28_marg88: Be not wise. He seems to have said the same as “lean not upon thy own prudence”. But he leans on his own prudence who puts what seems to him to be done or said before the decrees of the fathers; while he is wise in his own conceit who, in the things he has been able to know rightly from the teaching of the fathers, exalts himself above the rest as more learned. And what is the true wisdom of man he shows thus: Fear God, and depart from evil. It is like that in Job: “Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom: and to depart from evil, is understanding.” For the perfect ought so to keep themselves from all evils as always to call to mind with fear the presence of the divine majesty. And note that above he warns to have confidence in the Lord, but now to fear God. There he strengthens the minds of the weak with the promised help of God, lest they despair; here he restrains the stronger with the remembrance of the fear of God, lest they presume on themselves.
28_interl185: fear God, and there shall be health
28_marg89: For … health, etc. By the bones are signified the solid works of the virtues; by the navel, which is in the middle of the inner part of the body, the still weak and imperfect action of the good. If, then, thou fear God and, trusting not in thy own strength but in God, abstain from evils, both the weakness of thy work will grow strong to the state of perfection, and the strong works will receive that by which they may be strengthened yet more.
28_interl189: seek his praise, not thy own; otherwise thou dost not honour him
28_marg90: Honour, namely so that men, who are his handiwork, made to his image, may be renewed.
28_marg91: Substance, etc. Not only of the substance of money, which we give to the poor, but of all the good we do, of the grace we have received from the Lord. He too honours the Lord with his substance and the first of his fruits who ascribes whatever good he does not to himself but to him.
28_marg92: Thy barns shall be filled. “Lay up to yourselves treasures in heaven.” If the saints have treasures in heaven, because they find true riches there, they surely have there both barns and presses too, namely because “they shall no more hunger nor thirst”.
28_marg93: And in the present also the Lord sometimes grants as a reward greater gifts to be ministered to the teacher who ministers the bread of the word and the cup of spiritual grace to the needy. He who bestows earthly aid on the poor is made richer by giving, through the heavenly reward.
28_interl195: “I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear”
28_interl197: because these things are given thee by the Lord
28_marg94: Presses, etc. Because the inward sweetness of eternal things kindles the hearts of all the faithful in the praise of their Maker; for hence he says: “That you may eat and drink at my table, in my kingdom.”
28_interl199: lest the words of God be neglected
28_marg95: The correction. There are those who serve the Lord in prosperity and fall away in adversity. So wisdom, having taught him how to live in prosperity, exhorts him also not to faint under correction, lest, when sickness or poverty or the like comes, he lose the godliness he seemed to have in quiet times.
28_marg96: For whom the Lord loveth, he chastiseth. So much the less, then, ought we to murmur at the scourge with which we are chastised, the more surely we hold in it a pledge of a father’s love. Whence he himself says: “Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise.”
28_interl203: reject not correction, for blessedness is not to be without adversity; but blessed is the man that findeth wisdom
28_marg97: Blessed is the man, etc. Having comforted those placed under discipline and correction, he adds to what he had begun, suggesting that the true blessedness of man is not to be without the adversities of the present, but to rejoice in receiving eternal wisdom: which in this life is to know the will of the Lord, and in the life to come to enjoy the sight of him.
28_marg98: And is rich in prudence. Having said “that findeth wisdom”, he rightly added “and is rich in prudence”. For there are those who find wisdom by hearing the teaching of the truth with the ear, but neglect to be rich in prudence, being unwilling to open their hearts wide to take in its fulness.
28_marg99: Is better. Let him who has gained the riches of wisdom not fear the correction of want: the heavenly gift surpasses all treasures.
28_marg100: Chiefest and purest. Because “the root of wisdom is to fear the Lord”, these are the first and purest fruits; or because God, who is seen, is from the beginning, and nothing defiled meets the eye in the sight of him; or because man was first created for this contemplation, whence the first robe is given to the son returning to his father; or because gold that is first and unworked is commonly the purest. And our first robe is the blessedness truly to be believed, which is to be given back to us in the resurrection, but is promised more fully by the Lord.
28_interl205: not only than earthly riches but heavenly ones; nay, her brightness is preferred even to the very sight of the angels; whence: “For what have I in heaven? and besides thee what do I desire upon earth?”
28_marg101: Length of days, etc. By the sight of his Godhead he endows his elect with everlasting light, and in this present life he enlightens and strengthens the same with the sacraments and gifts of his incarnation; he gives to those who sell all they have to gain him “a hundredfold in this world, and in the world to come life everlasting”.
28_marg102: In the old translation of the Parables, after “riches and glory” there follows what our copies do not have: “Out of her mouth proceedeth justice, and she carrieth law and mercy upon her tongue.”
28_marg103: Her ways, etc. The actions and teachings contained in the gospel are beautiful, because they are divine and those of a pure man who never transgressed the law, and all his commands lead to eternal peace. All that he did in the flesh serves to reconcile mortals to God, to make peace between the human race and the angels, and to show his own the examples of peace and love to be kept towards one another.
28_marg104: As the tree of life was in the midst of paradise, so through the wisdom of God, which is Christ, the Church is given life; in the sacraments of his body and blood she now receives a pledge of life, and in the future she will be made blessed by the sight of him present.
28_interl210: in the present she gives life by his body and blood
28_marg105: The Lord by wisdom. Figuratively, by the Son he set the Church in the solidity of faith. He established the heavens by prudence when through him he enlightened the hearts of the lofty preachers.
28_interl215: “Thou hast made all things in wisdom, O Lord.”
28_interl216: according to the letter: and all things
28_interl219: according to the letter it is plain
28_marg106: By his wisdom the depths have broken out, in the days of Noe; or when springs and rivers daily flow out of the deep through the veins of the earth.
28_marg107: Otherwise. By wisdom the depths have broken out: the deep things of the heavenly sacraments, which by the gift of Christ’s grace are made known to the faithful. And the clouds grow thick with dew: namely the lofty masters of the Church, watering by their contemplation and life the hearts of their hearers, as the earth lying beneath them. They grow thick with dew because with the most delicate discernment they weigh their own virtues: by which they may make progress, by which they may seek the heights, and which they may show to the lesser for an example.
28_interl221: he warns that evil and its ways are not to be imitated
28_marg108: My son, let not … depart, etc. Take care that thou lose not the grace of wisdom, which is so great, wearied by temporal discipline.
28_interl222: “Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal.”
28_interl224: which says: “If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor.”
28_marg109: And there shall be life to thy soul. Thy soul has life with God if thou keep his decrees, though the flesh be pressed by the discipline of correction, or even of death.
28_marg110: And grace to thy mouth, etc. “How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth.” The mind’s understanding, then, has its own palate, with which it judges the words it hears, with which it weighs by discernment the things and deeds of each, and receives these by embracing them and scorns those by rejecting them. With this palate, when we keep the law and counsel of God, grace is multiplied; for the more skilfully anyone obeys the divine commands, the more sweetly he conceives his love, which the prophet, desiring it to be in us, speaks of: “O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet: blessed is the man that hopeth in him.”
28_marg111: Then shalt thou walk. We go confidently in our way when, trusting in the grace of God, we receive progress in our good manner of life. If, then, we humbly submit to his commands, we both reach the taste of heavenly love more sweetly with the palate of the mind and shall always gain an increase of good working. And in temptations too we are defended by his help, so that we do not faint. For this is what follows: “And thy foot shall not stumble”; for “to them that love God, all things work together unto good”.
28_interl226: thou shalt not faint in temptations
28_marg112: If thou sleep. It is plain according to the letter: he sleeps and wakes, rests and walks, in safety, who remembers that he lives innocently and justly before God. But the just man too, when he sleeps in death, not only does not fear the powers of the evil spirits, but rests in peace and safely awaits the day of resurrection, because he has God everywhere as his protector and keeper. Whence: “For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me.”
28_interl228: safely awaiting the day of resurrection
28_marg113: Do not withhold, etc. Having warned above that the law and counsel of the Lord be diligently kept, and promised eternal rest to those who keep them, he now goes over in many ways the things to be kept. First, returning to what he had broken off, he teaches that mercy is to be shown to our neighbour and that we must live justly with him; then he warns beforehand that we must beware of the enemy. Do not withhold, then, he says, etc., lest thou hear from the Lord with the Pharisees: “You yourselves have not entered, and those that were entering you have hindered.”
28_interl236: that is, do good and depart from evil
28_marg114: Say not, etc. Not only of almsgiving, but of all the commandments of Christ, who says: “You are my friends, if you do”, etc.
28_interl237: that is, against thy friend, however wicked
28_marg115: Strive not. He does not forbid striving against one who does evil, that he may be corrected; for what sure necessity compels is not done without cause. Nay, God, who says: “If thy brother sin against thee, reprove him”, himself wills that thou bring back one who strays to the way of truth as far as thou canst.
28_interl241: do no evil, envy not the unjust man
28_marg116: For every mocker, etc. For he is a mocker who either scorns to fulfil the words of God that he knows, or corrupts them by understanding and teaching them perversely. He too is a mocker who despises God’s promises as worthless and scorns the wrath of his severity as bearable; and he also who wickedly insults the simplicity of his neighbours. And so the divine justice rightly abhors every mocker of this kind. And it is well added: And his communication is with the simple; for the proud, while they mock the simple, judge themselves wiser than those they deride. But their wisdom, as James says, “is earthly, sensual, devilish”. But the Lord’s communication is with the simple, because he enlightens with the secrets of wisdom those whom he sees to have nothing of earthly pomp and double-dealing. Whence he says: “Thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones.”
28_interl243: imitate him not, for want is from the Lord
28_marg117: In the house of the wicked. Like the rich man clothed in purple, who in this life lacked spiritual things, and afterwards came to such want that he did not receive even the drop of water that he sought.
28_marg118: Whence: “Who hath blessed us with spiritual blessings in heavenly places, in Christ”; who at the reward will hear: “Come, ye blessed”, etc. But according to the letter too it often happens that those who plunder the goods of others are at last consumed by want, while those who give away their own abound even in earthly goods.
28_interl245: he will allow them to be deceived by Antichrist
28_marg119: The scorners, etc. James and Peter set down these verses according to the old translation: “God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.”
28_interl247: whence: “Every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted.”
28_interl248: because the promotion of fools is disgrace
28_marg120: Hear, ye children. From here, being about to exhort them to the love of wisdom, he explains how he himself was taught wisdom by his father.
28_interl249: the instruction of a father is to be embraced
28_interl252: despair not of wisdom, for I also
28_marg121: For I also, etc. Nothing raises minds more to the hope of gaining wisdom than when we remember that those whom we now admire as shining in wisdom were once little and untaught.
28_interl255: for the other died soon, as if he had never been
28_marg122: An only son in the sight. Why does Solomon call himself an only son in the sight of his mother, when Scripture testifies that a brother of the same mother went before him? Only because that one, soon after his birth, departed this life without a name, as if he had never been.
28_marg123: Let … receive, etc. He who reads over the Chronicles will find that counsels of this kind were given to Solomon by his father David.
28_marg124: Get. Remember to act wisely in all the good things thou possessest; or scorn all the earthly things thou possessest, so long as thou gain wisdom. This he himself did: for when the choice was given him, he put the love of wisdom before all things. In the Gospel, he who sought the precious pearl, when he had found it, sold all and bought it.
28_interl281: to the chief part of the mind
28_marg125: She shall give to thy head. It is plain of Solomon: when he despised all things for wisdom, having gained it he shone with a greater height of glory. But to our head too, that is, to the chief part of the mind, if we embrace wisdom, a fuller grace of the Spirit is added, and over and above, a crown of life will be given in the future.
28_marg126: Hear, O my son, etc. Having set out what he had received from his father, he returns to teaching the hearer the wisdom he had begun.
28_marg127: Hear. He warns him to receive his words.
28_interl287: that is, that thou mayst receive the gifts of eternal life
28_marg128: By the paths of equity. The paths, that is, the actions, of equity, when they are begun, seem strait and narrow; but when they make progress, they now seem spacious and wide from habit. The prophet bears witness: when he was beginning, he said to the Lord: “For the sake of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard ways”; afterwards, as he made progress, he sang: “I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart.” So though the paths of equity seem strait to thee when thou beginnest to enter them, when thou hast entered them the steps of thy mind will not be straitened; but thou wilt find, as the Lord says: “For my yoke is sweet and my burden light.” For the reprobate both enter on a broad road in this life and on the last day hear: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the exterior darkness”; but the feet of the elect will be directed “into the way of peace”.
28_interl290: by which paths of equity, when
28_interl293: as the wicked, who stumble in the middle of their course
28_marg129: And when thou runnest. The more eagerly thou runnest to fulfil the commandments of God, the less wilt thou fear the adversities that might hinder thee. For whoever toil in wicked action find a stumblingblock in the middle of their course, because, while they do not look ahead, they are suddenly snatched away to punishment.
28_interl298: enter her paths, but be not delighted
28_interl299: the subtle counsels of the wicked
28_interl301: let it not please thee, but flee
28_interl303: so eager are they for evil
28_marg130: In the doing of crimes the wicked take delight as in feasts they have won. Or indeed they drink the wine of the condemned, and rejoice to take away the ears of corn from the hungry, as Scripture testifies is the custom of the ungodly.
28_interl311: flee the paths of the wicked, for they are darkness; but the paths of the just
28_marg131: But the path of the just. The works of the just are done in the light of knowledge and lead to eternal life, which is the perfect day.
28_marg132: The way of the wicked, etc. Of them John the apostle says: “He that loveth his brother, abideth in the light, and there is no scandal in him. But he that hateth his brother, is in darkness, and walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth; because the darkness hath blinded his eyes.” Against which it is said above to the wise man that when he runs he shall not meet a stumblingblock.
28_interl318: but thou, lest thou fall with them
28_interl319: with the ear of the heart
28_marg133: My son, hearken. He warns that we must hearken to sound words and turn away from wicked thoughts.
28_marg134: With all watchfulness, etc. There are those who seem to men to live rightly; but because they do not act with a right intention, their life, which was believed good, is rejected as wicked by God, who looks on the heart. With all diligence, then, keep the cleanness of thy heart, because the manner of life is weighed by its judgement.
28_interl329: lest thou speak, or listen to one speaking
28_marg135: Remove from thee. Know that thou must keep it in two ways, so that thy mouth speak nothing froward: guard thy own lips, lest they grow used to detraction; and flee others whom thou knowest to be given to this vice, lest they corrupt thee.
28_interl333: he warned to keep the heart and the tongue; now the eyes
28_marg136: And thy eyelids. Learn diligently the road of justice by which thou oughtest to walk, and in all that thou plannest to do, carefully foresee to what end it will come. For this is for the eyelids of thy eyes that look straight on to go before thy steps: to reach by careful thought the good work one is about to do, and to foresee by meditation that it is according to God.
28_interl336: namely, lest thou err in deeds or in faith
28_interl337: make straight the paths, lest thou decline
28_interl338: lest they be moved from their purpose
28_marg137: Shall be established. Lest thou be moved from a good purpose by lightness of mind. Hence the Apostle: “Be ye steadfast and unmoveable; always abounding in the work of the Lord.”
28_marg138: Decline not. The right way is taken as the good one, the left as the reprobate. We are not forbidden, then, to walk in the right way, but to decline to the left. For he declines to the left who is unjust; he declines to the right who wants to claim for himself that he is just. He declines on the right who presumes on his own strength; he declines to the left who, because of his frailty, despairs of being able to be saved. He declines to the left who serves folly; he declines to the right who wants “to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise”. And the same is to be understood in like manner of the other virtues and vices.
28_marg139: Turn away thy foot, etc. That is, lest thou stray this way or that from what is right; for the virtues seek discretion, and every excess of them lies in vice.
28_marg140: If thou turn away thy foot from evil, if thou be eager to do, with the Lord’s help, the good things I have taught, he himself will be present, gracious to thy efforts, so that thou mayst both walk rightly now and come at last to eternal peace.
28_interl342: He chooses them: they please him. And so to those who displease him, the reprobate, he will say: “I know you not”; that is, I have not chosen you, you do not please me.
28_interl346: that thou mayst be able to come
28_marg141: My son, attend. Thus far he had chastened the hearer in general; from here, under the figure of a harlot, he forbids him the wickedness of the heretics.
28_marg142: Incline. The ear is to be inclined to wisdom, and the harlot to be fled, above all the fornicating woman.
28_interl347: by which thou mayst believe rightly
28_marg143: Thy lips. The lips with which thou professest the faith itself in simple, accustomed and ecclesiastical words. But according to the letter too, he who cleaves to a harlot defiles even his lips, by kissing or by doing shameful things.
28_marg144: For a honeycomb. For when, in the manner of the heretics, the sweetness of eloquence sounds forth not only to sufficiency but to overflowing, the falsehood, because it is seen to be openly uttered, is reckoned truth by fools.
28_marg145: The lips of a harlot. It is plain of the harlot, for she uses both sweetness of speech and beauty of body to catch the wretched.
28_marg146: Oil … her throat. The catholic faith is consecrated with the oil of the Holy Ghost; he shows his throat smoother than that who puts his own opinions before the faith of the fathers.
28_marg147: Her end, etc. A draught of wormwood turns bitter within, in the bowels; with a sword the limbs are struck from without. So, to show that the wicked in the last vengeance will be both filled with bitterness within and encompassed with everlasting punishments without, he declares that they are to be tormented with the bitterness of wormwood and cut off with the sword. And why the same sword is called two-edged the Lord reveals when he says: “But rather fear him that can destroy both soul and body in hell.”
28_interl357: the disgrace of vice is boundless
28_marg148: Wandering, etc. The steps of the heretics are wandering, for some deny that Christ is God, others that he is man, and the like; and this plague pours itself out into ways so countless that what they are cannot be traced out at all. But the catholic truth is not wandering and untraceable, for it is one and the same, acknowledged by all the faithful through the whole world.
28_marg149: Remove … far. The Apostle says: “Fly fornication”; for surely the first remedy for this vice is to be far from those whose presence either entices to the vice or helps it on. And for weak hearers too it is profitable to be wholly kept apart from listening to heretics.
28_interl360: by which thou art even the image of God
28_marg150: Give not to strangers, etc. Do not subject the honour in which thou wast created to the image of God to the wills of the unclean spirits, nor spend the span of living thou hast received at the pleasure of the cruel adversary.
28_interl365: for those who do wickedly labour
28_marg151: Lest, etc. Lest thou help on the deeds of the demons, by handing over either the wit of thy soul or the strength of thy body to the doing of crimes, and so, by adding thyself, increase another’s house, that is, the number of the lost. And he says well: thy labours be in another man’s house; for there are those who, as the prophet says, labour even to do wickedly; and would that it were unknown how much labour the heretics have undergone against the Church!
28_marg152: And thou mourn, etc. That is, keep thyself chaste for this reason, lest perhaps thou be forced to mourn in punishment, when not only the allurements of the flesh pass away, but, the body itself being left behind, the soul is compelled to give account for all it did through the body. And in this life too it often happens that those who squandered their goods in youth by living riotously fail through want in the time of old age; and when the heat of the flesh grows cold and the flower of youth withers, they see others enjoying the goods they had wantonly sold, and, groaning with a late repentance, they say what follows: Why have I hated.
28_marg153: Why have I hated. It is plain of the heretics in particular, for they could not be called back from error by the sayings and examples either of the old fathers or of the new.
28_interl371: by which the heretics are refuted
28_marg154: In the midst of the church. It is the same in Greek: an assembly of peoples. More precisely, however, “church” means a calling together, “synagogue” a gathering together. And the old people of God was indeed called by both names. But now, for distinction, that one is called the synagogue, ours the Church, by reason, namely, of its faith and greater knowledge; for things without reason can be gathered together, but only rational beings can be called together. Yet sometimes they are taken in an evil sense, as: “And a fire was kindled in their congregation”, and wrath; and: “I have hated the assembly of the malignant.” So the despiser of wisdom, when he considers his evils, seems to himself entangled in almost all evil; and this adds to the heap of evil, that he was not at the edge but in the midst, an example to others, even as an author of it; or at least that, placed in the midst of the body of the saints, he did not fear to lead a life foreign to theirs.
28_interl372: remove thy way far from her, but drink water
28_interl373: make use of the desire and services of thy own wife
28_marg155: Drink water. He teaches that we must beware of heretics and attend to the keeping and reading of the Scriptures. The knowledge, he says, which thou preachest to others, keep thyself, and be steeped in the watering of thy own words.
28_interl375: give thy son and daughters in marriage to others, and that openly, with many to witness
28_marg156: Let … be conveyed, etc. When thou hast kept it thyself, then preach to others also, and dispense the divine words to a great breadth of hearers according to the quality of each.
28_interl377: keep in thy power the marriages to which thou joinest thy children
28_marg157: Keep them, etc. We divide the waters in the streets and yet keep them to ourselves alone when we pour out our preaching widely without, and yet do not seek human praise by it.
28_marg158: Neither let strangers. The unclean spirits become partakers with the teacher if they corrupt his mind with pride while he preaches, or with heresy, or with any vice. But he alone possesses the waters who, faithfully joined with the members of the Church, keeps himself from strangers.
28_interl381: keep with the wife thou tookest when young as much temperance even when she has grown old, so that by the merit of faithful chastity thou mayst gain a blessing in thy offspring
28_marg159: Let thy vein be blessed. Let thy teaching, and whatever is born of it, be in the blessing of the Church; and rejoice with her to whom thou hast been joined from thy youth, that is, from the time thou believedst.
28_interl382: let her be thy dearest wife who, as the hind pursues serpents, pursues harlots and drives them from thy house; and let the son born of her be himself a lover of chastity, most agreeable
28_marg160: Thy dearest hind; or “most agreeable”, as some copies have it. It is holy Church, which crushes the serpent’s teaching. The most agreeable fawn is her people, delightful by the variety of its virtues; by her breasts we are inebriated when we are instructed by the pages of both Testaments against the deceits of the heretics.
28_interl383: hers, not another’s; for why art thou seduced?
28_marg161: Be thou delighted continually with her love. He does not teach us to be given up to love of a wife, but that thou take no other while the first lives, and never join thyself to a harlot.
28_interl384: by a woman, or a heretic
28_interl385: be not cherished in the bosom of another, for the Lord beholdeth
28_marg162: The Lord beholdeth. Let not adulterers think themselves covered by the darkness of night or by walls, nor heretics that their schemes can be hidden; “for darkness shall not be dark to the Lord, and night shall be light as the day”.
28_interl386: his steps, by which he is caught; for his iniquities
28_marg163: His own iniquities, etc. The sinner who has fallen into great crimes, or the wicked man in small ones, or the unbeliever; made anathema after receiving the faith, like the heretics; or catholics wrapped up in too many sins: these, bound by vices, or by the ropes of their sins, perish by the unceasing increase of their wickedness. For he who makes a rope always adds strand to strand by twisting and winding; such is the twisting of evil works, such are the books of the heretics, in which, knotting wrong to wrong, they do nothing by writing but bind themselves more tightly.
28_marg164: He shall die. Having discussed adulterers at length, he shows, after his manner, at the close of his account, what the end of such is: namely, that those who have hated the instruction of life are heading for eternal death.
28_interl388: by which the heretics hold themselves wiser than the holy fathers; or when the wicked, doing the works of darkness, think they are not seen by the Lord and can easily bear his wrath
28_interl389: whom thou hast taken into thy keeping
28_marg165: My son, etc. According to the letter it is plain, for he counsels him who has become surety for his friend to warn him earnestly, so that by paying back the money he owes the creditor he may free himself too. But otherwise, in this passage he instructs the teacher, and in the following one anyone at leisure, how he ought to behave. For it is said to the teacher: If thou be surety for thy friend, thou hast engaged fast thy hand to a stranger. Which is to say plainly: if thou hast taken up the soul of a brother at the peril of thy own life, thou hast now bound thy mind to the care of an anxiety that was not there before. Thou art ensnared with the words of thy mouth and caught with thy own words; for while thou art compelled to speak good things by preaching to those entrusted to thee, thou must first keep thyself what thou hast spoken.
28_marg166: Stir up. Remember not only to watch thyself by living well, but stir up him over whom thou art set from the sluggishness of sin by preaching.
28_interl395: by neglecting altogether the care of those under him
28_interl396: by not correcting them, out of weariness
28_marg167: He gives sleep to his eyes who neglects altogether the care of those under him. And he slumbers who indeed knows their blameworthy deeds, but through weariness of mind does not correct them with fitting rebuke.
28_interl400: with the wings of the virtues
28_marg168: As if to say: as a doe seeks to escape from the hand of one trying to catch her, so strive that, having taught thy hearer wholesomely, thou mayst escape free from the surety for his life. Or indeed, because the doe is by nature a clean animal, swift in running and very sharp of sight; whence in Greek she is called dorcas, from dercein, that is, from seeing. And a bird is wont to seek the heights by flying; so do thou, while thou art busy teaching those under thee, take care to be clean from all sins, active in good works, sharp-sighted in detecting the snares of the wicked, and safe on the wings of the virtues; so that, the work of preaching done, thou mayst deserve to fly across to things above and enter the pastures of heavenly life.
28_interl402: even if thou art not equal to teaching others, at least do not neglect the care of thyself
28_marg169: Go to the ant, O sluggard. Here he exhorts the man at leisure that, if he is not equal to teaching others, at least he not neglect to take care of himself; and if he cannot learn the wisdom of teaching from a man, let him learn the wisdom of working from the ant. Though she has no guide, nor master, nor captain, she provides her meat for herself in the summer and gathers in the harvest what she may eat. If so small an animal, lacking a captain, without reason, with nature for her guide, provides for herself for what is to come, much more oughtest thou, made to the image of God, called to see his glory, helped by such teaching of the doctors, having the Creator himself for thy guide, to gather in the present the fruits of good works, by which thou mayst live for ever in the future. This life is compared to harvest and summer, because now, amid the heats of temptations, is the time for gathering the merits of the rewards to come. The day of judgement is compared to winter, because no means will be left of labouring for life; but each will only be forced to bring out what he has stored from the barn of his former deeds.
28_interl403: if thou canst not learn it from a man
28_interl405: go to the ant, and how long
28_interl411: thou wilt be idle from good work
28_marg170: How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? How long wilt thou sleep in vices, O sluggard, when thou canst rise to work well; thou who, weighed down by harmful sluggishness, always sayest: I will lie a little longer, and so afterwards I will rise again by repenting? For it comes to pass that, while thou always puttest off good work, the judge who weighs thy deeds is suddenly at hand. For this is what follows: And … shall come upon thee, as a traveller.
28_marg171: Want, etc. It is plain according to the letter, for sloth is the nurse of want and penury.
28_marg172: Want and poverty are the last punishment, in which the damned merit nothing of riches; it will come as a traveller, because it is unforeseen and sudden.
28_marg173: But if thou be diligent. The earthly fruits we reap are compared not to a fountain but to a cistern, because they feed the gatherer for a time and in time fail. But he who has been diligent to labour for heavenly riches, the harvest of these will come to him as a fountain, because he will receive an unfailing reward for his labours.
28_interl418: “I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear.”
28_interl419: such is the diligent man; but a man that is an apostate
28_marg174: A man that is an apostate. He had spoken of heresy and other kinds of vice, had instructed the teacher, had stirred up the sluggard; but now he rebukes the schismatic too. Here note that the one he meant to call a sower of quarrels he first named an apostate; because, unless, like the proud angel, he first fell inwardly from the sight of the Creator by the turning away of his mind, he would not afterwards come outwardly so far as sowing quarrels. Of him it is rightly said: He winketh with the eyes, presseth with the foot; for it is the inward guard that keeps the outward members in order. So he who has lost the steadiness of his mind runs over outwardly in restless movement, and by the restlessness of his outward parts shows that he stands on no root within.
28_interl424: at all times he soweth discord, which God detests
28_marg176: Six things, etc. Of the same man he suggests how hateful to God it is to sow discord.
28_marg177: His soul detesteth. He speaks after the manner of men, to show that he greatly hates such people. Whence in Isaias: “My soul hateth your solemnities.”
28_marg178: Haughty eyes, etc. He lists six capital crimes, which nevertheless, in comparison with the sower of discord, he sets down as lesser, because that crime is greater by which the unity and brotherhood that is joined by the grace of the Holy Ghost is torn apart. For anyone may lift up his eyes boastfully, lie with his tongue, be defiled with murder and devise evils against his neighbour, subject his members to other crimes, bear false witness against someone (which is not to be thought the same as what he named above, a lying tongue: for a lie can be told, but not against a neighbour). Any lost man, I say, can bring evils of this kind on himself and others while the peace of the Church is kept. But what Donatus and Arius and their followers did is graver, for they rent the concord of brotherly unity.
28_interl432: to break unity, or the truth
28_marg179: Keep. Now, under the figure of an adulterous woman, he forbids listening to heresy.
28_interl438: fortify thy speech on every side with their sweetness, lest thou slip with thy tongue
28_marg180: Bind them in thy heart, etc. That is, hold the commandments of God fixed in thy thought.
28_marg181: When thou walkest. Let thy meditation on the divine law be so great that when, awake, thou art doing anything, thou turnest it over busily in thy mind; when thou sleepest, thou restest in the memory of it; when thou awakest, thou callest it first to mind with a busy mind. For so it will come about that thou neither stumblest when awake nor art harmed by the terror of the night.
28_marg182: Otherwise. When thou walkest in the progress of justice, let the commandments of God go with thee to instruct thee.
28_marg183: When thou sleepest. When thou sleepest in death, let them keep thy soul, lest the enemy seize it; when thou awakest in the resurrection, talk with them, awaiting the rewards that were promised thee if thou hadst kept them.
28_interl448: “Turn away thy eyes, that they may not behold vanity.”
28_marg184: Let not … covet. It is plain of the adulteress. But as for the heretics, if they seem to live well and behave fittingly, see that thou be not led astray by their teachings.
28_marg185: For the price of a harlot, etc. The pleasure of fornication is short, the punishment of the fornicator lasting. For as a fasting man, who went away filled after eating bread, escapes hunger for the day only, and nonetheless hungers afterwards; so he who goes in to a harlot for the hour lets his lust steam off, but after a little it comes back hotter.

28_marg186: Can a man. To read the books of the heretics is allowed only to him who is so firmly grounded in the catholic faith that he cannot be parted from it by the sweetness or cunning of their words.

28_marg187: Not so great. Theft is said to be no great fault, not in itself, but in comparison with a greater sin, that is, adultery. So it is said to Jerusalem, sinning more grievously: “Sodom is justified by thee”; not because Sodom committed no sins or few, but because Jerusalem committed more.
28_interl462: not only his goods, but also
28_marg188: Because the jealousy, etc. It is to be understood of the Lord too: for whereas he now spares the reprobate, he does not spare them in the day of death, nor yield to the prayers of those who cry to him too late, nor accept gifts, for which there is then neither time nor means. For he is jealous if anyone presumes to corrupt his bride, that is, the Church, or any faithful soul.
